EMPLOYEE WAGE AND WORKING CONDITIONS DISCLOSURE RIGHTS (LABOR CODE §§ 232, 232.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE
This document describes what California Labor Code §§ 232 and 232.5 say about an employer's ability to restrict an employee's disclosure of wage amounts and of information about working conditions, and about the express carve-out those statutes leave in place for an employer's proprietary information, trade secrets, and privileged information. It is provided for information about Jordan Lee's and Acme, Inc.'s rights and obligations under those statutes; it does not itself instruct either party on what to do in any specific situation.

WAGE-AMOUNT DISCLOSURE: WHAT AN EMPLOYER MAY NOT DO
California Labor Code § 232 prohibits an employer from doing any of three things regarding an employee's disclosure of the amount of the employee's own wages: requiring, as a condition of employment, that the employee refrain from disclosing that amount; requiring the employee to sign a waiver or other document purporting to deny the employee the right to disclose that amount; and discharging, formally disciplining, or otherwise discriminating against an employee who discloses that amount. The statute's prohibition runs specifically to an employee's own wage amount — it does not, on its face, address an employee disclosing a co-worker's wage information obtained from the employer in confidence, a distinct scenario this clause does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "No employer may do any of the following: (a) Require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing the amount of his or her wages. (b) Require an employee to sign a waiver or other document that purports to deny the employee the right to disclose the amount of his or her wages. (c) Discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses the amount of his or her wages."
  — California Labor Code § 232, Cal. Lab. Code § 232 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=232.)
  Known gap: All three quoted prohibitions come from a single statutory section, Labor Code § 232, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) — they are treated here as one source, not three independent ones. The statute's own text does not define what counts as a "waiver" sufficient to trigger subdivision (b), nor does it specify a private civil remedy, penalty, or enforcement mechanism for a violation; this clause does not address how a violation of § 232 is enforced (for example, through a Labor Commissioner complaint, a private lawsuit, or another avenue), because the statute's own text is silent on that question and no separate enforcement statute was researched for this document. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

WORKING-CONDITIONS DISCLOSURE: WHAT AN EMPLOYER MAY NOT DO
A separate statute, California Labor Code § 232.5, extends a parallel set of three prohibitions to an employee's disclosure of information about the employer's working conditions generally, rather than only wage amounts. An employer may not require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing information about the employer's working conditions; may not require an employee to sign a waiver or other document purporting to deny the employee that right; and may not discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses such information. The statute does not itself define "working conditions," and this clause does not address where that term's boundaries lie.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "No employer may do any of the following: (a) Require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing information about the employer’s working conditions. (b) Require an employee to sign a waiver or other document that purports to deny the employee the right to disclose information about the employer’s working conditions. (c) Discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses information about the employer’s working conditions."
  — California Labor Code § 232.5, Cal. Lab. Code § 232.5(a)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=232.5.)
  Known gap: All three quoted prohibitions come from a single statutory section, Labor Code § 232.5, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) — they are treated here as one source, not three independent ones. As with § 232, the statute's own text does not specify a private civil remedy or enforcement mechanism for a violation of these three subdivisions, and this clause does not address enforcement. A CourtListener search for case law construing § 232.5's working-conditions prohibition specifically (as opposed to § 232's wage-disclosure prohibition) returned only tangential results — cases citing the section in passing among a longer list of claims, without construing its terms — so no case law is included in this clause. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

THE STATUTE'S OWN CARVE-OUT FOR TRADE SECRETS, PROPRIETARY INFORMATION, AND PRIVILEGE
Labor Code § 232.5 contains its own express limit on the working-conditions disclosure right it creates: the same section states that it is not intended to permit an employee to disclose the employer's proprietary information, trade secret information, or information that is otherwise subject to a legal privilege, without the employer's consent. This carve-out sits within the same statutory section as the working-conditions disclosure protection described in a companion clause of this document — the protection and the carve-out are two subdivisions of one section, not separately enacted provisions. Labor Code § 232, the parallel wage-disclosure statute described in another companion clause, contains no equivalent carve-out in its own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "This section is not intended to permit an employee to disclose proprietary information, trade secret information, or information that is otherwise subject to a legal privilege without the consent of his or her employer."
  — California Labor Code § 232.5(d), Cal. Lab. Code § 232.5(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=232.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Labor Code § 232.5(d); it is the same statutory section as the wageconf_workingconditions_disclosure_prohibition clause's subdivisions (a)-(c), so the two clauses are not independent sources of each other. The statute's own text does not define "proprietary information" or state how this subdivision interacts with California's separate Uniform Trade Secrets Act definition of "trade secret" (Civil Code § 3426.1(d)), and this clause does not resolve that interaction — it states only that § 232.5 itself uses the broader, undefined phrase "proprietary information" in addition to "trade secret information." No case law construing this specific subdivision was located: a CourtListener search returned only cases mentioning § 232.5 in passing without construing subdivision (d), so none is cited here. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

A CALIFORNIA COURT'S RECOGNITION OF A PUBLIC-POLICY WRONGFUL TERMINATION CLAIM
In Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc., a California Court of Appeal addressed a marketing director who alleged she was discharged after discussing bonus amounts with coworkers. The court held that the employee had a right, rooted in public policy and grounded in Labor Code § 232, to join in a discussion with other employees about whether they were being equitably compensated, and reversed summary judgment against her wrongful-termination-in-violation-of-public-policy claim. The court's holding treats § 232 as more than an internal wage-disclosure rule: it treats the statute as capable of supplying the public-policy basis for a separate common-law tort claim for wrongful termination, distinct from any claim under the statute itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "We conclude that the employee had a fundamental right rooted in public policy to join in a discussion with other employees about whether they were being equitably compensated. Labor Code section 232 prohibits the discharge of employees for discussing the amount of their wages."
  — Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc., 99 Cal. App. 4th 1361 (2002) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2285001/grant-burton-v-covenant-care-inc/)
  Known gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision from one district (Second Appellate District, Division One), decided in 2002; this clause does not address whether other California appellate districts, or the California Supreme Court, have independently addressed the same public-policy question, and no further case-law search beyond this decision and its own citations was performed. The decision itself quotes a version of Labor Code § 232(c) that included additional language ("for job advancement") not present in the current, currently-operative statutory text quoted elsewhere in this document — consistent with the statute having been amended by Stats. 2002, Ch. 934, effective January 1, 2003, shortly after this opinion issued; this clause quotes only the court's own reasoning about the public-policy right, not the court's quotation of the now-superseded statutory language, to avoid misstating the current text of § 232. This clause does not address whether the same public-policy reasoning would extend to § 232.5's working-conditions disclosure right, which the court did not consider. The opinion was retrieved via the CourtListener API (opinion id 2285001) on 2026-09-08 and the quoted text was confirmed as an exact contiguous substring of the retrieved html_with_citations field, stripped of markup.

"WAGES" UNDER § 232 REACHES BEYOND BASE PAY
The same Grant-Burton decision addressed what "wages" means for purposes of § 232's protection, in a case where the disclosed information was a discretionary bonus rather than base salary. The court held that § 232 protects an employee who discloses "wages" as that term is broadly defined elsewhere in the Labor Code to include all amounts for labor performed, and on that basis concluded that the bonuses at issue — tied to increases in patient count or facility growth — came within the statute's protection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Section 232 protects an employee who discloses his or her “wages,” which is broadly defined to include “all amounts for labor performed.”"
  — Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc., 99 Cal. App. 4th 1361 (2002) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2285001/grant-burton-v-covenant-care-inc/)
  Known gap: This clause describes one Court of Appeal decision's application of the term "wages" to one specific category of compensation (facility-growth-linked bonuses); it does not address how the same reasoning would apply to other forms of compensation such as equity, commissions, or benefits, which the court did not consider. The quoted passage itself cross-references Labor Code § 200, subdivision (a)'s definition of "wages" rather than restating it in full; that separate statutory definition was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so this clause relies on the Court of Appeal's own characterization of it rather than on independently confirmed statutory text. This clause is a companion to wageconf_public_policy_tort_recognition, drawn from the same single opinion; it is not an independent corroborating source for that clause's public-policy holding. The opinion was retrieved via the CourtListener API (opinion id 2285001) on 2026-09-08 and the quoted text was confirmed as an exact contiguous substring of the retrieved html_with_citations field, stripped of markup.

WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT COVER
This document addresses only Labor Code §§ 232 and 232.5 and the single Court of Appeal decision described above. It does not address other, separate California statutes that also touch employee pay disclosure and transparency — including Labor Code § 1197.5 (equal-pay and pay-history provisions), Labor Code § 432.3 (pay scale disclosure in job postings), or the federal National Labor Relations Act's separate protection for concerted activity among employees discussing wages — none of which is described here. It also does not address the corpus's separate documents on trade secret misappropriation, the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, or the Silenced No More Act (Government Code § 12964.5) and the settlement-confidentiality statute (Code of Civil Procedure § 1001), each of which concerns different statutory confidentiality restrictions from the ones described here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
I, Jordan Lee, acknowledge that I have received and reviewed this description of Labor Code §§ 232 and 232.5 and Acme, Inc.'s related practices.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
